title: Inherited Roth IRA: the 10-year rule
audience: Adult children of retirees with Roth IRAs, and retirees planning their beneficiary designations
thesis: Most non-spouse beneficiaries must empty an inherited Roth IRA within 10 years. The Roth's tax-free growth makes the timing decision consequential.

concepts.label: The 10-year rule
concepts.body: Per SECURE Act 2.0 (effective 2020), most non-spouse beneficiaries must empty an inherited IRA by the end of the 10th year following the original owner's death. Withdrawals are still tax-free for a Roth — but the empty-by rule is hard.

concepts.label: Strategy: wait until year 10
concepts.body: Strategy 1: wait until year 9, then withdraw everything in one lump sum. Tax-free for the Roth. Captures the maximum tax-free growth window. Drawback: one year of large income could push the beneficiary into a higher tax bracket for unrelated income (Social Security, dividends).

concepts.label: Strategy: spread over years 1-10
concepts.body: Strategy 2: spread withdrawals over years 1 through 10, taking ~10% per year. Smooths the tax impact, but loses some of the tax-free growth. The Roth stays tax-free either way — the only cost is opportunity cost on withdrawn dollars.

sources: IRS Notice 2022-53 — proposed regulations on the 10-year rule
